Chapter 3: Facing the Realities of Gender and Power
Have you ever noticed how, in some homes, the unspoken rules about who gets to speak up, who makes the decisions, or who gets to dream, feel like they’re written in invisible ink? No one sits down and spells them out, but somehow, everyone just knows.
Picture a daughter watching her brother come and go as he pleases, while she’s expected to stay close to home. She sees how her mother’s opinions are brushed aside, how her aunt’s ambitions quietly fade, and when she asks questions about love or marriage, all she gets are warnings about honor and shame.
The truth is, these patterns aren’t unique to one family or even one community. They’re woven into the everyday fabric of so many Muslim societies—reinforced by religious leaders, cultural traditions, and social expectations. The message is loud and clear: men lead, women follow. Men protect, women obey. Men are seen as the guardians of faith, while women are expected to be its keepers.
But under the surface, there’s a simmering frustration. Imagine a young woman—talented, driven—dreaming of becoming a doctor. Her father is proud, but he’s also anxious. He worries what the neighbors might say if she spends too much time outside the home. Her mother, who once had dreams of her own, tells her to be patient, to wait for the right husband, to put her family first. And so the daughter is left feeling torn—pulled between loyalty to her family and the hope of living a life that’s truly hers.
Somewhere else, a group of women gathers in a tiny apartment to share their stories. Some wear headscarves, some don’t. Some are married, some aren’t. But all of them know what it’s like to be told what they can or can’t do, to be judged for their choices, to feel less than. They talk about how religious texts are used to keep them out, and about the fear that comes with questioning the status quo.
Most people don’t realize just how deeply these patterns run. They’re reinforced by sermons, by what gets taught in school, by the offhand comments of relatives and neighbors. And when you ask why things are the way they are, the answers are usually vague, circular, or just not there at all.
Here’s what’s important to remember: the real issue isn’t with faith itself, but with how it’s interpreted and enforced. The Qur’an, when read with an open heart, speaks of equality, compassion, and justice. But too often, those verses get overshadowed by interpretations that protect the interests of those in power.
There’s a powerful moment when a mother shares her long-lost dreams with her daughter. She remembers a time when anything felt possible, before the weight of expectation settled on her shoulders. And as the daughter listens, she realizes her own struggle isn’t just hers—it’s part of a much bigger story. A story of women told to wait, to sacrifice, to accept less.
The path forward? It isn’t easy. It calls for courage, persistence, and the willingness to ask tough questions. Questions about why men and women are assigned certain roles, about how power is divided, and about what’s really lost when everyone stays silent. It’s about seeing that true faith isn’t about blind obedience, but about standing up for justice.
Change doesn’t always start with grand gestures. Sometimes it’s a quiet conversation between mother and daughter. Or a group of friends daring to share their stories. Or a young woman deciding she won’t accept the limits placed on her. Over time, these small acts of resistance add up, slowly building the possibility of a new way forward.
A way where faith and freedom aren’t at odds, but walk hand in hand.
